## Positioning & Offer

Tim Burley creates distinctive, trademark-ready names that boards align behind and lawyers can register. Work spans company and brand names, post-merger naming, sub-brands and naming architectures, products and SaaS platforms, property and place names, and typefaces.

Two ways to work together:
- **For Agencies (https://www.timburley.com/brief?route=agency):** Specialist naming plugged directly into design, brand or digital agency projects without carrying permanent naming headcount. Seamless client-facing collaboration alongside strategists, designers and account leads.
- **For Direct Clients (https://www.timburley.com/brief?route=direct):** Direct access to the person doing the naming, from strategy brief through shortlist workshops and alignment alongside your trademark attorney.

## Commercial Model & Process

- Typical timeframe: 4 to 6 weeks from strategy brief to trademark filing.
- Commercial structure: Fixed-fee engagement scoped once the brief and approval pipeline are agreed.
- Three ingredients: (1) One senior namer (no junior hand-offs), (2) An agreed approval pipeline set before naming starts, (3) Independent trademark attorney clearance (your IP partner handles formal registration; Tim pre-screens candidates to cut wasted legal spend).

Five-stage funnel:
1. **Strategy & territories (The brief):** Agree commercial strategy, audience, naming territories and decision-makers.
2. **Long-listing (~1,000 to ~100 names):** Deep linguistic, metaphorical and contextual exploration edited down to ~100 strong candidates.
3. **Shortlisting (12 to 15 pre-screened names):** Checked across UK/EU/US registers, domains and social handles before presentation.
4. **Selection (3 to 4 favourites):** Presented to the smallest viable deciding group to prevent committee dilution.
5. **Clearance & filing (1 registered name):** Independent trademark attorney pre-registration report and filing support.

Four watchwords: Simple, Memorable, Meaningful, Protectable.

Four name types (the aviation spectrum):
1. Literal / Descriptive (e.g. British Airways)
2. Experiential / Suggestive (e.g. Virgin Atlantic)
3. Associative / Metaphorical (e.g. Monarch)
4. Abstract / Arbitrary (e.g. EasyJet)

## Clear Boundaries (Four Things This Practice Does Not Do)

- **No AI name-slop buckets:** No raw LLM prompt dumps of 400 derivative words. Every candidate passes human taste, commercial context and trademark judgement.
- **No junior hand-offs:** You brief, challenge and decide directly with Tim Burley from start to finish.
- **No amateur legal advice:** Formal registration belongs with a qualified trademark attorney; Tim prepares clean, registrable shortlists alongside them.
- **No bloated 90-slide theatre:** Clear criteria, disciplined territories, rigorously edited shortlists and straight-talking decision guidance.

## Common Questions (FAQ)

### How much does a brand naming project cost?
Every engagement is quoted as a clear fixed fee based on the variables in your brief: the number of names and any existing brand architecture, whether it is for a company, product, service, place or other application, the depth of trademark clearance and international linguistic screening needed, domain and handle constraints (such as requiring an exact-match .com), the nature of the business including regulatory compliance requirements, stakeholder complexity and turnaround. Working directly with an independent specialist also keeps fees free of large-agency overheads. Once we agree those essentials and your approval pipeline, I send back a straightforward fixed-fee proposal before any work begins.

### How long does a brand naming project take?
Most projects take four to six weeks from the agreed strategy brief through to handing a cleared shortlist to your trademark attorney. That covers strategy and territories, long-listing, pre-screened shortlisting and alignment workshops. Tighter launch windows or multi-market clearances are scoped upfront.

### Should I hire an independent naming consultant or a branding agency?
Working directly with an independent specialist gives you twenty years of hands-on naming craft without agency layers or junior hand-offs. It also means your visual identity or brand rollout can stay with your existing design studio or internal team, built on a distinctive name that boards can align behind and lawyers can register.

### How do brand, design and digital agencies work with you?
Agencies bring me in as a specialist naming partner so they can offer senior naming leadership without carrying permanent headcount. I work alongside your strategists, designers and account leads, either directly in the room with your client or behind the scenes, delivering pre-screened candidates that give design teams strong strategic ground to build from.

### Can you register our trademark, or do we still need a trademark attorney?
Formal searches, legal opinions and trademark filing always belong with a qualified trademark attorney. My role is to understand UK, EU and international trademark registers well enough to pre-screen candidates before you ever see them, cut wasted legal spend and keep three or four genuinely registrable front runners alive for your IP partner.

### Why shouldn’t I just use AI to name my business or product?
AI is brilliant at finding the average, and great names never come from there. Prompting an LLM produces familiar category clichés that routinely collide in trademark classes and dilute distinction. Choosing a lasting name still takes commercial judgement, cultural awareness, legal foresight and the human alignment to get a whole room behind one confident decision.

## Six Naming Pitfalls (Summary)

### 01. The Thunderbolt Fallacy
- Pattern: “I don’t know what I want, but I’ll know it when I hear it.”
- Why it happens: Chances are you won’t recognise the right name in a flash of lightning. Worse, when a name does suddenly grab you out of nowhere, it is usually because it subconsciously reminds you of something else that already feels familiar, not because it is uniquely right for your business.
- How the process prevents it: We replace vague gut-instinct waiting with a clear, agreed brief and distinct strategic territories, so you know exactly what a name is supposed to achieve before you judge it.

### 02. The Negative Filter
- Pattern: Appraising every new name by hunting for reasons not to like it.
- Why it happens: It is always easier to defend a safe, literal name like British Airways than an evocative, distinctive one like Virgin Atlantic. Looking through a negative filter surfaces criticisms that may be technically true yet strategically irrelevant, pushing teams steadily towards predictable, uninspired choices.
- How the process prevents it: We evaluate names for what they can unlock, not merely what can be nit-picked. Every shortlist is weighed against long-term brand distinctiveness rather than fear of minor objections.

### 03. The Working Title
- Pattern: Quietly falling in love with a temporary placeholder name.
- Why it happens: Because a temporary placeholder starts out with zero stakes, the team uses it every day, gets comfortable with it, and gradually pours real meaning into it. By the time genuine launch names arrive, they feel strangely foreign next to the old habit.
- How the process prevents it: We surface attachment to internal working titles right at the start and judge every candidate, including any existing placeholder, against the same objective commercial and trademark criteria.

### 04. The Straw Poll
- Pattern: Plotting names from “boring” to “bonkers” and putting it to a group vote.
- Why it happens: Dressing naming up as a democracy almost guarantees the safe, least-worst middle ground wins. Majority votes naturally cancel out bold ideas, sacrificing creative vision just to keep the largest number of people mildly comfortable.
- How the process prevents it: Gathering input is valuable; delegating the decision to a popularity contest is fatal. We lock down an approval pipeline upfront, clear on who inputs, who agrees, and who holds the final decision.

### 05. The Front Runner
- Pattern: Falling completely in love with one early favourite to the exclusion of all others.
- Why it happens: When a team pins all its emotional energy on a single early favourite, a blocked trademark class or unavailable domain sends the entire project crashing back to square one, with morale bruised and deadlines blown.
- How the process prevents it: We keep three or four genuinely strong contenders alive through formal screening and legal partnership with your trademark attorney, so clearance stays calm, decisive and cost-effective.

### 06. The Rational Focus
- Pattern: Judging a name purely on dry, logistical checklists.
- Why it happens: Pronunciation, spelling, global translation and trademark clearance are essential hygiene factors, but they are only half the equation. Judging exclusively on rational metrics strips away the emotional resonance that turns a functional label into a brand people actually believe in.
- How the process prevents it: We balance legal and practical rigour with human feeling and story, knowing when a name should be evocative, and when a clear name (like South West Food & Drink paired with “Sensational”) comes alive through the narrative around it.

## Named Projects (14 Case Studies, Reverse Chronological)

> Note: Case study narratives below are written in the first person by Tim Burley.

### 01. Cora (2025) · Healthcare
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/cora
- Summary: Naming the combined healthcare organisation formed by the merger of two established UK providers: Healthshare and Connect Health.
- Client: Healthshare & Connect Health
- Agency partner: R&D Partners
- Domain: corahealth.co.uk
- Trademark: Registered (Classes 9, 41, 42, 44; https://trademarks.ipo.gov.uk/ipo-tmcase/page/Results/1/UK00004121477)
- Brief: Robin Jaffray and Tim Doust, the senior agency leaders behind the brand consultancy R&D Partners, brought me in to lead name development for the merger of Healthshare and Connect Health. Working alongside R&D, creative specialists and the leadership teams from both legacy organisations, we needed a single unifying name that honoured what patients already valued while giving the newly combined business a warm, credible platform for growth.
- Naming story: Reviewing patient feedback across both businesses revealed one consistent theme: people deeply valued the personal level of treatment they received and the genuine commitment to patient wellbeing. A short, memorable female name gave us an immediate human presence, while “Cora” also carries a natural etymological root back to the human heart. Together, those qualities created a warm, personal, unmistakably caring name for the merged organisation.
- Process & clearance: I developed and presented the shortlist across both leadership teams, guided stakeholder alignment past legacy-brand attachment, and worked directly alongside the company’s legal partner to secure formal trademark registration prior to launch.
- Outcome: Cora launched cleanly with trademark protection in place, giving the combined organisation a compelling, human brand name that stands apart from clinical healthcare conventions.

### 02. Hemiko (2023) · Energy
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/hemiko
- Summary: Naming a national low-carbon district heating force following private-equity investment and spin-out from Pinnacle Group.
- Client: Hemiko (formerly Pinnacle Power)
- Agency partner: Organic
- Domain: hemiko.com
- Trademark: Registered (Classes 4, 35, 36, 37, 39, 40, 42; https://trademarks.ipo.gov.uk/ipo-tmcase/page/Results/1/UK00003923225)
- Brief: When a private equity firm acquired Pinnacle Power, the business needed to step out from the wider Pinnacle Group and chart an ambitious independent course. Working directly with the client leadership, we set out to create an innovative, distinctive name capable of establishing a major British force in district heating.
- Naming story: “Hemiko” grew from the concept of Heat Energy Markets (HEM), capturing a forward-looking vision of how communities can both generate and consume low-carbon heat locally. While district heating has long been established across continental Europe, Hemiko needed a fresh, modern name built to champion its growth across the UK.
- Process & clearance: Following PE investment, the new company required rapid alignment across investors and management alongside clean trademark clearance, giving the spun-out business a scalable name free of legacy utility baggage.
- Outcome: Hemiko has gone on to establish itself as a leading investor, developer, maintainer and operator of UK town- and city-scale heat networks.

### 03. Corigan (2021) · Technology
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/corigan
- Summary: A confident, standalone name for an enterprise SEO platform, cleverly rooted in an anagram of its parent agency, Organic.
- Client: Organic (SEO platform)
- Agency partner: Organic
- Domain: corigan.io
- Trademark: Registered (Classes 9, 35, 42; https://trademarks.ipo.gov.uk/ipo-tmcase/page/Results/1/UK00003717279)
- Brief: Corigan was built as a powerful search engine optimisation platform supporting SEO teams working on larger enterprise clients. Most search-tech tools default to predictable descriptive variations on “Search” and “Rank”, blending into an undifferentiated sea of lookalike software names.
- Naming story: Developed while I was working at the digital agency Organic, the platform needed the confidence to stand on its own feet and build independent brand equity, while preserving a meaningful thread back to its creators. The solution was hiding in plain sight: “Corigan” is an anagram of “Organic”.
- Process & clearance: By avoiding literal category descriptors, Corigan sidestepped crowded trademark classes and gave the platform immediate personality and authority in client pitches without being tied down to parent-agency dependency.
- Outcome: A crisp, confident platform brand with an insider origin story: distinctive in a noisy MarTech category, legally ownable, and built to grow on its own terms.

### 04. Yomira (2021) · Luxury
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/yomira
- Summary: A bespoke, ownable start-up name for a luxury superyacht charter company serving high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients worldwide.
- Client: Yomira
- Agency partner: R&D Partners
- Domain: yomira.com
- Trademark: Registered (Classes 12, 35, 36, 39; https://trademarks.ipo.gov.uk/ipo-tmcase/page/Results/1/UK00003538653)
- Brief: Working again with Robin Jaffray and Tim Doust at R&D, we partnered with Yomira’s two founders, Neil and Amanda, to create a brand name capable of entering an exceptionally demanding international luxury market, curating tailored superyacht charter experiences for discerning travellers exploring the world’s oceans.
- Naming story: Yomira was coined by bringing together “Yo” as a contraction of “your” and “Mira” derived from the Sanskrit for ocean, literally evoking “your ocean”. It captures the promise of a voyage designed entirely around the individual client, without ever lapsing into nautical clichés.
- Process & clearance: In a crowded global luxury market, securing both legal distinctiveness and clean digital ownership was vital. Creating an ownable coined mark enabled us to secure yomira.com and build a brand foundation with real international poise.
- Outcome: Yomira gave the new venture a distinctive, creative and effortlessly international name, equally at home on a superyacht masthead, digital flagship and global luxury press.

### 05. Gwallon Keas (2019) · Property
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/gwallon-keas
- Summary: A deeply rooted Cornish place name for a Devonshire Homes residential development, bridging regional identity with genuine local heritage.
- Client: Devonshire Homes
- Agency partner: Believe in
- Domain: N/A
- Trademark: Unregistered
- Brief: When Devon-based housebuilder Devonshire Homes embarked on a major residential development in Cornwall, there was an obvious local sensitivity: the fierce friendly rivalry between Devon and Cornwall. Generic invented developer names would have felt imported and tone-deaf.
- Naming story: We dug into the local history and Cornish legend around the site. We uncovered “Gwallon” (referencing a local standing stone) and “Keas”, meaning an agricultural plot or field. Bringing them together created “Gwallon Keas”: an authentically Cornish place name rooted in the land that the new homes emerge from.
- Process & clearance: By leaning wholeheartedly into genuine Cornish roots rather than glossing over geography, the development earned local credibility and stood proudly on its own two feet. It was one of numerous development names we created for Devonshire Homes.
- Outcome: Gwallon Keas gave the new neighbourhood a rooted, respectful identity built to endure alongside the community for generations.

### 06. With Energy (2018) · Energy
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/with-energy
- Summary: A single, human-first community energy brand designed to deploy seamlessly across multiple neighbourhoods.
- Client: Community energy provider
- Agency partner: Believe in
- Domain: with.energy / withenergy.co.uk
- Trademark: Unregistered
- Brief: Building directly on the relationship from Loka, the client wanted a standardised energy brand that could drop into many different communities across the country, eliminating the need to invent and register a separate brand for every local scheme.
- Naming story: “With Energy” turned a simple, disarming preposition into a flexible brand platform. It worked both as a clear company name and as a collaborative statement about working with local communities, bringing warmth, momentum and enjoyment to how people engage with their local energy provider.
- Process & clearance: Engineered as a repeatable naming solution able to flex cleanly across diverse developments and resident audiences without losing personal warmth.
- Outcome: With Energy created an approachable, scalable brand architecture built to travel cleanly from community to community.

### 07. Grain (2017) · Technology
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/grain
- Summary: A William Blake-inspired broadband brand bringing hyper-fast full-fibre connectivity to new-build housing communities.
- Client: Pinnacle Group joint venture
- Agency partner: Believe in
- Domain: grainconnect.com
- Trademark: Registered (Classes 9, 37, 38; https://trademarks.ipo.gov.uk/ipo-tmcase/page/Results/1/UK00003214453)
- Brief: Created at Believe in for a joint venture between a property group and a telecoms provider, Grain was built to challenge legacy telecoms giants, partnering with housebuilders to install end-to-end fibre-optic networks directly into new residential developments.
- Naming story: Because the network installed fibre from end-to-end, we drew inspiration from “To see a World in a Grain of Sand”, the opening line of William Blake’s poem, “Auguries of Innocence.” Silicon becomes optical fibre, hair-thin strands of glass capable of carrying vast bandwidth into modern homes. “Grain” gave the business a poetic, genuine origin story right as full-fibre was taking off, without tying the brand to jargon that would quickly date.
- Process & clearance: Pairing an evocative, human lead word (“Grain”) with a clear functional anchor (“Connect”) gave housebuilders and residents immediate clarity while standing miles apart from hyperbolic telecoms clichés.
- Outcome: Grain continues to connect thousands of new-build homes across the UK to ultrafast broadband.

### 08. FS Silas (2016) · Type
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/fs-silas
- Summary: Naming and shaping the espionage-themed launch story for a new slab-serif and sans-serif typeface pairing from Fontsmith.
- Client: Fontsmith (acquired by Monotype)
- Agency partner: Believe in
- Domain: N/A
- Trademark: Unregistered
- Brief: Fontsmith was one of the world’s leading independent type foundries prior to its acquisition by Monotype. At Believe in we launched several typefaces for the firm, including FS Silas, which included the naming, launch identity, type specimen, print support and promotional imagery.
- Naming story: We built the name and launch campaign around a crisp theme of espionage and intrigue, framing the typeface launch like a classified secret dossier supported by teaser print materials and specimen artefacts. “Silas” carried the exact air of quiet intelligence, literary poise and sharpest graphic character needed for the letterforms themselves.
- Process & clearance: Typeface names live permanently inside designers’ font menus worldwide, so the name had to sit naturally within Fontsmith’s “FS” foundry architecture.
- Outcome: FS Silas launched with memorable creative intrigue and remains part of the celebrated Fontsmith library under Monotype.

### 09. Loka (2015) · Energy
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/loka
- Summary: A community-focused low-carbon energy brand created for Knight Dragon’s Greenwich Peninsula district heating network around the O2 in London.
- Client: Knight Dragon
- Agency partner: Believe in
- Domain: loka.energy / lokaenergy.com
- Trademark: Registered (Classes 4, 35, 36, 37, 39, 40; https://trademarks.ipo.gov.uk/ipo-tmcase/page/Results/1/UK00003069008)
- Brief: Created for urban regenerator Knight Dragon, Loka serves the major residential and commercial redevelopment surrounding The O2 London on Greenwich Peninsula, operating from a central energy centre delivering heat across the entire community.
- Naming story: District heating is often presented in dry, technical utility language. “Loka” brought together the two defining truths of the network in one short, approachable word: “local” and “low carbon”, communicating both dedicated neighbourhood service and meaningful carbon reduction.
- Process & clearance: We shaped a name that could live effortlessly alongside ambitious urban architecture while feeling transparent, modern and trustworthy to residents receiving their energy bills every month.
- Outcome: Loka continues to serve customers across Greenwich Peninsula today, proving that low-carbon infrastructure can carry warmth and clarity.

### 10. Ockery (2015) · Food
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/ockery
- Summary: A characterful, ownable consumer seafood brand name rooted in coastal heritage, simplicity and wholesome recipes.
- Client: Ocean Crown
- Agency partner: Believe in
- Domain: ockery.com
- Trademark: Registered (Classes 29, 30; https://trademarks.ipo.gov.uk/ipo-tmcase/page/Results/1/UK00003138532)
- Brief: Seafood producer Ocean Crown (owned by Scandia Foods) needed a new consumer brand for a range of fishcakes made from fresh, honest ingredients and simple recipes.
- Naming story: “Ockery” emerged as a rich, tactile phonetic word with historical connections back to a traditional stone dwelling, instantly evoking roots, coastal simplicity and back-to-basics provenance.
- Process & clearance: Crucially, its distinctiveness meant it cleared cleanly and allowed us to secure ockery.com, giving the product range an ownable, memorable home on shelf and online.
- Outcome: A uniquely British, grounded food brand name brimming with warmth, texture and natural culinary honesty.

### 11. Uprising (2014) · Food
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/uprising
- Summary: A playful, rebellious challenger name for a gluten-free pastry brand built to spark a better-baking movement.
- Client: Independent founder
- Agency partner: Believe in
- Domain: N/A
- Trademark: Registered (Classes 29, 30; https://trademarks.ipo.gov.uk/ipo-tmcase/page/Results/1/UK00003061985)
- Brief: Created at Believe in for a founder who was fed up with tough, tasteless gluten-free pastry and had perfected a bespoke blend of gluten-free flours for delicious quiches, pies and baked goods.
- Naming story: Free-from food brands too often sound medicinal or apologetic. “Uprising” flipped that on its head with a joyful double meaning: the literal lift of great pastry rising in the oven, paired with the grassroots energy of a category rebellion, something coming up from the ground to disrupt a stale aisle.
- Process & clearance: Designed to feel playful, spirited and full of campaign potential rather than a dietary compromise, giving the brand an unmistakable voice from day one.
- Outcome: Uprising delivered a witty, energetic starting point for a challenger food brand built to rally gluten-free bakers.

### 12. Shape Mendip (2013) · Public sector
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/shape-mendip
- Summary: An adaptable, active name for Mendip District Council’s multi-agency hub bringing shared public services together under one roof.
- Client: Mendip District Council
- Agency partner: Believe in
- Domain: N/A
- Trademark: Unregistered
- Brief: Created for Mendip District Council while I was at Believe in, the initiative centred on a shared physical hub at the council’s headquarters where multiple public and partner organisations could come together under one roof to serve local residents.
- Naming story: Because the hub was designed to flex and evolve as different partners and providers joined over time, “Shape” worked on two powerful levels: an adaptable form that changes around community needs (echoed directly in the flexible identity), and the active civic purpose of shaping a supportive place where people want to live.
- Process & clearance: Multi-agency public-sector projects can easily stall into committee compromises. A clear strategic rationale kept partners aligned behind an active, plain-English name rather than administrative jargon.
- Outcome: Shape Mendip gave the shared-services hub an enduring, purposeful identity rooted squarely in the community it serves.

### 13. Meddo (2012) · Property
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/meddo
- Summary: A warm, reassuring brand name evolved from “meadow”, bringing calm and approachability to property maintenance.
- Client: Meddo
- Agency partner: Design Stable
- Domain: meddo.co.uk
- Trademark: Registered (Class 37; https://trademarks.ipo.gov.uk/ipo-tmcase/page/Results/1/UK00002614794)
- Brief: Created while I was at the brand consultancy Design Stable, the client was bringing together local property maintenance specialists united by a commitment to genuinely positive customer service, in a sector dominated by stiff, overly buttoned-down trade brands.
- Naming story: We wanted customers to feel they could breathe easy and know their home was in safe hands. That led to the calm, restorative image of a “meadow”; the alternative spelling created a modern, ownable, warm and distinctive brand that sat apart from traditional maintenance firms.
- Process & clearance: The distinctive spelling unlocked clean brand ownership and planted a light, human seed that carried effortlessly across the wider visual identity and launch rollout.
- Outcome: Meddo established a lighter, friendlier and far more engaging presence in a traditionally functional market.

### 14. South West Food & Drink (2004) · Public sector
- Case study URL: https://www.timburley.com/work/swfd
- Summary: A unifying regional brand name championing food and drink across the South West of England, proving that sometimes the obvious solution is the right one.
- Client: Taste of the West
- Agency partner: Red Rocket
- Domain: southwestfoodanddrink.org
- Trademark: Unregistered
- Brief: Food promotion group Taste of the West commissioned the agency Red Rocket to create a new unifying brand to champion food and drink from across the South West of England, backed by funding from the Regional Development Agency (RDA).
- Naming story: Sometimes the obvious solution is the right one. Rather than forcing cleverness onto a regional body that needed immediate clarity and authority, “South West Food & Drink” united producers and buyers under a name that was clear, honest and right. To accompany the main brand, we created a launch campaign built around the word “Sensational”, grounded in research showing that people strongly associated the region with tourism and memorable experiences, connecting South West food and drink to the sensations people enjoyed and held on to when visiting.
- Process & clearance: Effective naming requires the judgement to know when plain-English clarity beats invention, and how to strengthen a straightforward name with supporting narrative and campaign thinking that gives it genuine emotional pull.
- Outcome: South West Food & Drink established an unmistakable unifying flagship for the region’s producers, brought vividly to life through a “Sensational” launch rooted in memory, taste and sense of place.
